CAP07.overview: A language-driven task layer must refuse or ask rather than guess, and a safety supervisor must be independent of the stack it supervises and proven by fault injection.

CAP07.task: Build an LLM-free parser, a bounded planner, a behaviour tree with at most two retries and a safety supervisor with a hazard table, then run the CAP07 acceptance suite. State assumptions, a baseline, a boundary case, and a check that could reject your result.

CAP02.overview: A firmware-in-the-loop drive base turns portable C (speed loop, protocol, watchdog) into a tested wheel layer that the whole capstone stands on.
CAP02.application: Build the C core, call it from the simulator through ctypes, and prove step response, protocol and watchdog behaviour with an acceptance suite.
CAP02.task: Build a small reproducible example. Implement a PI wheel-speed loop, a CRC-8 frame codec and a watchdog in C, log a step response and a silent-host test, and calibrate odometry. State assumptions, a baseline, a boundary case, and a check that could reject your result.

CAP03.overview: Localisation fuses odometry, gyro and landmark detections in an EKF, and consistency statistics tell you whether its uncertainty can be trusted.
CAP03.application: Calibrate the simulated camera, detect wall markers, run an EKF on seeded trajectories and audit it with NEES and NIS.
CAP03.task: Build a small reproducible example. Implement an EKF with a range-bearing landmark update, a Joseph-form covariance and a gate, run seeded trajectories with ground truth and compute NEES and NIS. State assumptions, a baseline, a boundary case, and a check that could reject your result.

HW13.overview: Robot motors come in a few families (brushed, brushless, stepper, servo, linear) and each needs a transmission; the right choice depends on speed, torque, backdrivability and holding behaviour, not on one headline number.
HW13.application: Pick candidate motor families and a transmission for a drive wheel, an arm joint, a gimbal, a printer axis, a lift or a legged joint, and check a real product against one working point.
HW13.task: Build a small reproducible example. Write unit conversions, a joint fit check, reflected inertia, stall current and a self-locking test in Python and compare four real products against one working point. State assumptions, a baseline, a boundary case, and a check that could reject your result.

HW14.overview: A motor or gearhead datasheet is a set of measured points, limits and constants under stated conditions; reading it well means converting units, deriving the missing rows and trusting the continuous rating, not the stall value.
HW14.application: Read the sheet of a DC or brushless motor, a stepper, a smart servo, a planetary gearhead and an encoder, and check a motor and gearhead pair against torque, current and temperature limits.
HW14.task: Build a small reproducible example. Write a datasheet calculator for unit conversions, stall current, mechanical time constant, thermal derating, a gearhead limit check, a stepper current rise time and an encoder rate, and test it on real sheet values. State assumptions, a baseline, a boundary case, and a check that could reject your result.

HW15.overview: Motor sizing turns a task into numbers (force, torque, speed, duty) and then checks motor, gear ratio and driver against each of them: peak torque, heat, speed left under load, inertia ratio, stall current and back-EMF headroom.
HW15.application: Size a wheel drive, an arm joint and a lead-screw axis, and end with a motor class, a ratio, a driver and a list of checks that passed.
HW15.task: Build a small reproducible example. Reproduce the three worked designs in a Python sizing calculator and size a differential-drive robot of your own from two real datasheets. State assumptions, a baseline, a boundary case, and a check that could reject your result.
